utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon at this first hearing in 2009. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're ready to call our next witness, Dr. John Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I thought you would give us an opportunity to wish everyone the best for the year to come in his personal life and in his health irrespective of the positions we are in and the roles we are playing in this courtroom. That's one. Although I have taken notice that you are ready, Mr. Margetts. A few other matters which I would like to briefly raise, this being the following: We have come to a point in relation to the 54 bis application and decision taken on that and further reports received since then that the Chamber would like to receive from the parties their views on where we are now should there be any further orders or is this -- has the matter been concluded until now. The Chamber would like to receive submissions from the parties, if possible, within one week, to give your views on what the Chamber is expected further to do in relation to this application. That's one. Then, second, apart from the issue of what I could call the Pittman letter, we have received a letter on 29th of December in which applications are made even though not for the first time, at least. These are more or less applications rather than claims in relation to confidentiality. And before the Chamber would decide on the matter, the Chamber would like to give an opportunity to the parties to make submissions on the requests, applications, whatever you call it, made in the letter of the 29th of December, in response to the Pittman letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, first, I'm not sure if we should be in private for session for that or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have not given any further details specifically for that reason. But if you know what letter I'm talking about, then the only thing I revealed is that it's 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I know the letter of which you speak. I think it was the 19th, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have written down, it the 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think the letter is dated the 19th, but I could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I could be wrong as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it's again the Rule 70, Rule 54 bis matter which is raised in that letter, and the Chamber before where we earlier may have responded to a claim, we feel that we are now more or less invited to decide on a certain matter, and the Chamber would like to receive submissions by the parties on that matter, if possible, the matter is known to the parties, within still this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do need to clarify exactly what you would like submissions on so ... there was an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we go into private session please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to be clear, of the first two submissions will be written submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we expect them to be written submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Margetts, you're ready to call your next witness. We'll proceed because there's still, of course, a motion pending on the -- still a motion pending on the admission of the expert report --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of the next witness. The Chamber has decided that on the basis of the objections raised until now, it will not decide not to admit the expert report and that we'll proceed on the basis that the Chamber will consider admission and -- of course, the Chamber will write down the reasons why it does not accept the objections which are mainly based in the -- when given notice et cetera. Well, the whole -- the main reasons for objecting against the admission of the report. That is denied. We'll give the reasons in writing, and we'll proceed on the basis, although no final decision has been made yet on admission of the report, but we'll proceed on the basis that the Chamber seriously considers admission of the report, which still allows for critical questions which might change your mind as far as admission is concerned. But the matter raised has not given us a reason not to admit the report until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There is yet another issue, Mr. President, besides that. And that is obviously taken from the decision by the Office of the Prosecutor to move ahead with Dr. Clark's testimony at this juncture while the appeal on the adding the 189 additional victims in their clarification schedule is pending before the Appellate Chamber. As I had outlined previously, we had prior to that additional 189 victims. We had spent almost 3.000 hours investigating the various homicides -- or killings. I don't want to say homicides. Deaths that had been set forth prior to the 189 coming in. Now we're at a fork in the road because we have Dr. Clark, and if I take it from the Prosecution's plan and the evidence they intend to present, evidence concerning some of those 189 individuals is going to be presented to Dr. Clark. Now, one or two things can happen or would happen. One, on the appellant side all of that 189 list is stricken, and all his evidence is stricken as well. Or, two, if the Appeals Chamber sustains the Trial Chamber's decision, we, of course, will be coming back and ask for -- I can't believe it would be less than a three-month delay to investigate the 189 murders that the Office of the Prosecutor decided to move forward with. I will say that will unquestionably bring to bare bringing Dr. Clark back for additional testimony, if need be, once that investigation has concluded. So I present that, Judge, because, of course, on behalf of General Gotovina, we don't want to waive any positions, but I also wanted to be completely candid with Your Honour that to a certain extent we are prepared to cross-examine, but we certainly haven't, although I have touched on it, we certainly have not come near doing the proper investigation on -- on another 189 deaths that have been presented. So that's where we are. If the Prosecutor chooses to move forward to led evidence on those 189, which I'm sure they have given what I've seen in their evidence to be presented, that's going to trigger a sequence of events that we will revisit at a later date, should the Trial Chamber's decision be sustained. Of course, if it is not sustained, we will move to strike all of that evidence as well as all testimony that the Prosecutor now -- is now attempting to elicit from Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your position is perfectly clear that the Chamber is put on notice that there may be an application, depending on the circumstances, what the Appeals Chamber will decide. That you would, also depending on what kind of evidence is elicited from the witness by the Prosecution, that there's a fair chance that you would ask for more time and for Dr. Clark to be re-called.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, you're ready to call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that will be Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: That will be Dr. John Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Mr. Clark. Before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher, and I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: John Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could please have 65 ter 6498 presented on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Larger documents take a while now and then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can imagine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, we're still waiting for the Croatian version to appear on the screen. But if you look at that first page there, do you recognise that as your curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if we can just scroll through that so Dr. Clark can confirm each page of that document. And Dr. Clark won't need to read each page. It's just a question of him recognising that is his recent update of his curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, is that your completed curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if this document could please be given an exhibit number and entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given exhibit number P1250. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1250 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, can you please confirm that you are a forensic pathologist of 24 years standing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And you're currently occupying the position of consultant pathologist to the University of Glasgow?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Consultant forensic pathologist, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And between 1999 and the year 2001, you acted as the chief pathologist, forensic pathologist, engaged by the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY to conduct autopsies of bodies exhumed in Bosnia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, in regard to the bodies that you exhumed when you occupied that position of chief forensic pathologist, how many different grave sites were those bodies exhumed from?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I think there were about seven main areas throughout the Balkans, which includes Bosnia, Croatia, and briefly in Kosovo. Within each of these areas, there were quite a number of separate sites, so likely Srebrenica sites, there must have been at least half a dozen different sites that we looked at. In Croatia in Eastern Slavonia, we looked at a number of different sites there. So all in all, probably about 15, 16 graves, specific grave sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And were also some of those grave sites located in the Drina valley, and were some located in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And of those 15 to 20 sites, how many bodies were exhumed and how many bodies would have you been responsible for the forensic analysis of the remains of those bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact figure, but I think it is around about 3.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Dr. Clark, just in respect of the Croatian exhumations, it is correct, isn't it, that you were involved in examining the remains that were exhumed from the Knin cemetery for a period of about six weeks between the 14th of June, 2001, up to the 27th of July, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, in late October last year, you were requested by the Office of the Prosecutor to produce an expert report in relation to your forensic examinations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if I could please have 65 ter 6453 presented on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, you'll see on the screen the first page there. Is that the first page of the report that you produced?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if we could move to the last page and Dr. Clark could see the final page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Dr. Clark, is that your signature that you see on that page and the date there, the 11th of November, 2008. Is that the date you completed the report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if this report could please be given an exhibit number marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's to be marked for identification for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given exhibit number P1251, marked for identification. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it keep that status for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Clark, in the course of your preparation to give evidence today, did you review this report, and are there any parts of it about be that in the body of the report or alternatively in the annexes that you'd like to correct or clarify?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: There's the very occasional grammatical error with a comma perhaps missed but not important. There's only one -- I think it is on -- if I can look at my own file?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If a hard copy is available for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On page 12, this is a list of the Annex A cases for KN01, and the seventh case down, which is 236 B, you'll see on the fifth column under minimum number of shots, I have a figure 4. That should actually just be 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark. Are there any further clarifications or corrections?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Nothing of -- of great importance, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Clark, I'd now like to refer you to page 2 of the report, and it's the second-last paragraph on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if that page could be shown on the screen. And Dr. Clark is referring to that in the hard copy of his report that he has brought with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And -- yes, it's the last paragraph that appears on the screen. And there's a reference there to the last sentence of that last full paragraph appearing. It says that: "Revised numbers are given in the discussion of the individual graves, but as an initial guide, of the 295 bodies, 245 were probably 'true' cases ... and true is in inverted the commas ... and of the 94 body parts, perhaps about 50 appeared to be relevant." Now can you explain to the Court what you meant when you referred to cases as true cases?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Within the sites particularly there KN02 and KN03, there were bodies which had no injuries in them, which appeared to be hospital patients because they were wrapped in hospital sheets or had other hospital-related items, and we took the view that these were probably people who died of mainly natural causes in hospital and should probably be excluded from analysis of the other findings. We may have misinterpreted that, but that's the view I took.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And when you arrived at the conclusion that other cases were true cases, what type of indicia indicated to that you they were true cases?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: These were cases which appeared to be people that had not died in hospitals. In other words, they had normal clothing on them. They had -- a lot of them -- well, the majority of them had trauma. And for considerable number of the bodies, particularly -- mainly in KN01, there were photographs of them at -- before burial and clearly showing that they were not hospital patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark, for that clarification. Dr. Clark, just for clarity I'd like to just go through the numbering system that appears in your report and in the annexes to your report. And can you confirm that the bodies were exhumed from the Knin cemetery and they were exhumed from four separate areas of the Knin cemetery and these different areas were given the reference KN01 through to KN04?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And can you further confirm that where bodies were exhumed, the letter B was affixed to that number; and where body parts were exhumed, the letter BP was affixed to the number?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And each of the bodies exhumed from those four locations was given an individual number?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, in -- well, yesterday, you met with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, and you've also had the opportunity in meetings with the Office of the Prosecutor in December to go through the autopsy reports which are relevant to the victims that are listed in the annexes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And I'd like at this stage, Mr. President, to bring up 65 ter 6779 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This seems to be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, has it been released in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It may be possible for us to present a hard copy of that document. I have a copy of the document in my possession. It's merely -- sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we've had some success.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And Dr. Clark, if you could look at the left-hand side of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if you could just go through the four pages of this document. And, Mr. Registrar, if you can just scan down, and if you could reduce the size of that so that Dr. Clark can see that full depiction of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Clark is that your signature that you see there, and is that today's date?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And does this list represent a listing of the autopsy reports relevant to the bodies that are referred to in the annexes of your report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if this document can please receive an exhibit number and be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I received this morning. Obviously it was signed by Dr. Clark this morning. I don't know about the accuracy of these numbers. We have any number of problems with the numbering system in these documents. So at this juncture I'm not prepared to concede that this document is an accurate assessment of these numbers that we have been dealing with today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that you had no possibility to verify whether the information is correct. Well, first of all, of course we have numbers; and second, we have the testimony of the witness that these are the relevant ones. Is there any objection against admission as such? Of course you can ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My objection to the admission is the accuracy of the document if we can just MFI at this point and have a little time to check the accuracy, I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, any problem in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no problem with that. Just one matter that I may raise at this stage, and that is that these autopsy reports have already been admitted into evidence by the decision of the Trial Chamber of the 28th of November, 2008. So, Mr. President, you are completely correct in characterizing this as the witness's testimony as to the accuracy of those numbers and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- it might be a good idea to give at least some time since the document has been disclosed very, very recently. If there are any objections against which would affect the probative value such as numbers not to be found anywhere that at least an opportunity is given to the Defence to verify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, this document marked for identification would receive number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this document shall be given exhibit number P1252, marked for identification. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it keeps that status for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Clark, in your expert report you refer to a team of people that you were working with or you were leading as chief pathologist in the mortuary examining the bodies exhumed from the Knin cemetery. And you mentioned that that team consisted of about 20 people. That's at page 3 of your report. And then at page 25 of your report, the last page, you list the names of pathologists who prepared autopsy reports. Could you just outline to the Trial Chamber who the members of the team were and their functions. And in a moment after you have done that, in general terms we will then refer to one of the autopsy reports, and we'll go through the report with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. Clearly an exercise of this sort requires a lot of different specialisms to be involved. Bear in mind this is just simply in the mortuary. This is nothing to do with the grave site. So at any one time we would have three pathologists working, and they would be working with anthropologists. There would be a photographer taking evidence, photographs. There would be scenes of crime officers recording documents and clothing, et cetera. Then there would be other people. Radiographer, various mortuary technicians which were assisting with the bodies. People washing the clothes, and there would be secretaries typing the reports. So it was quite a sizeable team but worked together, and there were good systems in place. The pathologists themselves, I had the job of recruiting these, and over the whole season which wasn't just in -- in Croatia. I tried as much as I could to recruit pathologists from as many different countries as I could. So you'll see in the list on the last page that we have two pathologists from South Africa, both with considerable experience of gunshot injuries, and then we have the others are from Europe, from Portugal, from the Czech Republic, and from Poland. They were not all present at the same time but three -- there would be three, including myself, present at any one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd now like to present for illustrative purposes one of the autopsy reports to Dr. Clark. It is it not presented for any specific reason other than it's a typical autopsy report and evidence sheet and then just go through the documents in these autopsy reports with him to indicate at what stage of the examination these documents were produced and who produced them. It will be a lot easier for us to do that with a document in hard copy. It would be easier for Dr. Clark to identify the pages as I think for the parties to follow. I have the 65 ter, and it can be produced on the screen as well. But if the court usher could assist me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection against the use of hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, this is 65 ter 6189, is the autopsy report, and the evidence sheet, which is the second document, is 65 ter 6190. So if we bring up 65 ter 6189 at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now this is the autopsy report for a case identified as KN01/223 B, and the reference to this case appears in Annex A to Dr. Clark's report which is page 12 of his report, and it is the fifth case down in Annex A, and there's a cause of death which is described as gunshot injury, face. Dr. Clark, I'd like you to look at this report, and if you could, to describe to the Trial Chamber the process once the remains were brought to the mortuary, the activities that the team engaged in, the documentation they had in their possessions and which members of the team were responsible for which part of the examination and for filling out which -- filling out which pages of this documentation.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Okay. I think the easiest thing to do is to ignore the first three typed pages and go straight on to the fourth page which is 825 which is the first one with writing on it. The document from here on was the working document for each of the pathologists. What would happen would be that a body would be removed from the fridge and logged on various tables in the mortuary. The very initial examination would be that it would be fluoroscoped, that is a sort of form of X-ray done in the presence of the pathologist, and that was simply a screening exercise to look for any metal fragments, particularly bullets. The findings of that were recorded on page -- sorry, I should know this by heart. Is recorded on 828. Top half of the page which says injuries, fluoroscopy findings. So in this case the initial examination revealed no bullet fragments or no significant bullet fragments in the remains. So that was written on the page there. The next page is going back to 825, and this is an initial very general description of the remains. Just on opening the body-bag what did we see. So we would describe as it skeletonised remains or an intact body or soft tissues. It was a very general observation. And we would also at this stage record the metal identification tag which was present in the majority of bodies. Having done that, the -- and any photographs taken as necessary, the body is then -- the clothing is removed, any clothing on the body and other items is removed but not recorded by the pathologist at this stage. I'll come back to that. This is on page 826. What we do record, however, was if there was any blind fold or ligature on the body and anything other relevant with the remains. In this particular case, there was nothing. Next page is 827. This is a tick sheet to indicate as much as we can, bearing in mind these are largely skeletonized remains, what we can tell. Build, whether it was male or female, build, hair colour, anything else. In most of these cases, it was impossible to tell any of these things. Then the main work is described on 828. This is the body -- the bones have been washed and the body is cleaned and laid out and with the assistance of the anthropologist, the pathologist and anthropologist would work together to look at the bones, reconstruct where necessary, and to identify particular injuries. And once we had done this, the pathologist recorded that on page 828, the bottom half. So this was under head and neck. This lady clearly had a gunshot injury to her face and neck, and I have described it. It is in scribbly writing, but this is done in a mortuary and will be tidied up at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Dr. Clark, could you just indicate to the Court the distinct roles played by the anthropologist and the forensic pathologist.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: The anthropologist in an exercise like this has an invaluable role because their expertise is looking at bones. So they do two things. First of all, they examine the bones, put any broken bones together to -- particularly those that have been injured to see if there was any particular pattern of injury to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Clark, may I interrupt you for a second. You just referred to this lady where you earlier drew our attention to the -- to the pages where we find the tick boxes, where the person is described as a male. So I was a bit confused by --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry about that. This is a good example -- yes, it is a man, I'm sorry. For some reason I think we had chosen an earlier case which was a woman, and this is indeed a man. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, may I invite you to very much focus on the case before you when answering questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This man clearly had an injury to his face and neck, a gunshot injury, and we were able to describe it in some detail, and describe the direction of the injury. This appeared to us very much an injury which had occurred in life, and we can argue about the reason for that in due course if need be, but that is hence the tick of antemortem. Moving on to the next page, which is 829, we obviously look at the whole body. And you'll see that this page is blank because there were no injuries in the trunk. That is the chest and abdomen. No broken ribs, no nothing. So that is left blank as are the two sections on the next page, which is 830, under arms and legs. So this man, his only injury was -- was to the head and neck. In this particular case, his body was -- was well preserved, and we were able to look at the internal organs. This was very unusual, but from time to time it was present. And we were able to tell at the very least that this man had gallstones. That is totally irrelevant in the cause of death, but it was there. The next page, 831, is where we record any bullets or shrapnel which we have removed from the body. In this case, there was none. That does not go against a gunshot injury, I hasten to add. But there was no bullet fragments left in the body. There are other tick sheets there. The anthropology, there was no samples taken for that. The -- on every case we took a sample for DNA analysis to assist in future identification and that was typically the femur and the tooth. And these were samples which were generally taken by the mortuary technicians under our guidance. There were no other items were retained. And so with that, that's the end of the pathologist's examination. At the same time there are two -- well, actually three, detachable sheets at the back of the report. This is 835, 836, and 837. I'll come back to 832 later on. These are sheets for the anthropologists, and we would -- the pathologist would give these pages to the anthropologist and ask that they complete them with such information as sex, estimated age range, estimated stature because this was again part of their remitt and specialism. They also did -- this is 836. They also did a complete inventory of the bones present. And 837 is an examination of the teeth when they were present. These three pages, that's 835 to 837, once completed by the anthropologist, would be given back to the pathologist, and armed with that, and also armed with the body recovery report, which is 838, this is a report prepared at the field, at the grave site, which was made available to us, so with that, with the anthropology findings and with other own findings we then completed page 832, which is the summary and conclusions. Again you will see it is sort of scored out and what have you, but this was done usually within the next few days in the peace and quiet of an evening or weekend by the pathologist who would bring together all the findings and write it down in this -- in this fashion and would also give a formal cause of death at the end and then sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, there is one other matter that I'd like to refer to you to, and that is the evidence sheet. That is not part of this document but is part of the second document. And if you could describe at what juncture this evidence sheet is compiled and the relevance that has to the pathologist's ultimate report.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: The only relevance -- and these were sheets prepared by the scenes of crime officers. The only relevance is in the last page which is a colour photograph of the clothing. And I forgot to add that before our conclusions, we went back to the clothing which was now washed and laid out in the way that you can see in the last page of the -- of the document, which is 6547. The pathologist would look at this clothing not for any identification purposes, that was done by the scenes of crime officers, but to look for any damage to it, like gunshot holes any burning or any other finding, and that would be inserted in page -- the second page of our report, which is 826.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Dr. Clark, if could you move to the first three pages of the autopsy report. That's 822 through to 824.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. Once we had completed the conclusions on 832, then the whole report -- all the pages were given to the secretaries, and they typed up in the standard format all the findings which was able to be brought down to a three-page document, which you have here. In this document, the conclusions and cause of death are given on the first page, and the other findings are listed in the other two pages. But if you compare the two the typed report and the handwritten report, you will find them -- exactly the same information in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, there is one final page that we haven't dealt with, and that's the last page of the autopsy report, and that is the body recovery report at 838.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I did mention that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. If you could just go through that with me -- with us, with the Trial Chamber again, just to indicate who prepared the body recovery report and where was that prepared.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: These were sheets, single sheets, prepared by the team exhuming the body at the grave site. They made this sheet available to us in the mortuary so that we were able to look at it when we were doing both examination and the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, unless there are any questions or further clarifications that, Mr. President, you or Your Honours would seek from the witness, then I'm going move on to some exemplar illustrative photographs of some of the remains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one question for you. On what basis would it be established that teeth would be fractured post-mortem or antemortem by ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be the appearance of them. It is not always easy to distinguish the two, what is caused before and after death. If it was a fracture of the tooth caused long after death, then it is fairly obvious because the surfaces are a white surface. In this case, it was decided that the injuries to the teeth -- we don't actually identify injury to the teeth as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, 24 odontogram fractured -- fractured post-mortem, 38 fractured post-mortem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I follow that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 837.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see odontogram, and I see on the top right-hand list of 8 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see them now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I see 24 fractured post-mortem. I see 38 further below, I see fractured post-mortem as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This sheet was filled out by an odontologist or at least an anthropologist specializing in dental work, so this is his or her document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. Of course, the reason for my question is that if a body apparently received important injuries antemortem, and if it was then buried, of course I'm wondering what caused teeth that are relatively strong, isn't it, to be fractured after that moment, and if it was on the same day of the burial, what would explain the distinction between half an hour before or half an hour after. Of course, I'm also asking myself when there are such injuries to the face, whether it's not more logical to expect that when these injuries were inflicted, whether it would not have the teeth have suffered from it as well, where apparently are the teeth on one side, if I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm afraid I can't answer to this. Did I not complete the sheet. So I'm not sure what the anthropologist meant. I fully accept that, yes, it is likely that a gunshot injury to the face would cause damage to the teeth. So I'm not entirely sure what is meant there, I'm afraid. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Clark, are you able to explain to the Trial Chamber how you can determine whether bones are broken post-mortem or antemortem is there any differences in the way that the remains appear?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: It can be very difficult. A bone which is broken long after the death as in when the body is being exhumed or even within the mortuary, that would have a distinctive appearances. The edges would be white, and we could easily distinguish that. I accept that it is very difficult to distinguish an injury which is caused just before death and which potentially was the cause of death with an injury which could be caused in the hours or even few days afterwards. I have tried to explain that in the -- in the report, and the difficulties we have for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, since we're focussed on this case, I do have two photographs relevant to this case. I hadn't informed the Defence that I had intended to present these photographs because, in fact, I hadn't intended to present them, but it may be, in light of the Chamber's questions, may be useful to see the skull and to see the contemporaneous photograph. utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I hate to take issue with my learned friend. But I did receive later on last night a series of photographs, and I have attempted to ascertain whether, in fact, I -- the Gotovina Defence had received these photographs, and frankly the production on photographs was quite spotty, so given what we were attempting to do in preparing for this, I don't know if we have these photographs, if we have not, given the fact that I received this disclosure late last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.text: The photographs that were sent over yesterday evening are a difficult category of material as to these two photographs. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to keep matters short. There are I would say two possibilities. The one being that the photographs that we expect to be shown by Mr. Margetts show clear differences by what we have seen on paper. Then it might give an additional opportunity to the Defence to challenge whatever is in the paper or on the photographs, or it is more or less the same, then it's an illustration, not more or less. Would it be worthwhile to do such an exercise, of course, giving an opportunity to looking more closely at the photographs, once so, perhaps mark them for identification for the time being and then see whether you detect anything that could assist the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I appreciate that, that guidance. The exercise is simply having an opportunity to take a look at it before we engage in -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... it goes without saying, Mr. Kehoe, that Mr. Margetts should have -- should have -- indicates to you that he wants to use these photographs and at least refer to numbers, if they had been disclosed already, and if not yet been disclosed to -- to give you copies of it. Well, let's not start telling whether the year started good or badly, but if there are any objections from other Defence counsel in relation to this. Then let's have a look at the photographs which will be marked for identification, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could please have 65 ter 6793 presented on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Clark, this is a photograph of the remains or at least the skull and other bones of the body marked KN01/223 B. And can you indicate to the Trial Chamber by reference to your conclusions the extent to which you relied on your examination of this skull in reaching the conclusions that you reached.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, this -- to me at least anyway, this shows a very clear injury typical of a gunshot injury with the entrance probably on the left side of the lower jaw immediately above the letter N, the gap there. The -- there is fracturing -- destruction and surrounding fracturing of the lower jaw round about, and the bullet has then travelled backwards and has damaged the bones of the neck, the spine which are the bones laid out at the side, the right side. You can see that they are fractured. So this looked to me like a gunshot injury which had gone through the lower jaw to the left of the midline, back through the lower part of the face, and had come out at the neck.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could have an exhibit number, please, for the autopsy report, which is 65 ter 6189, which is for KN01/223 B and also -- and just for that document. utterances.text: So we don't need a number for that.

utterances.text: Yes, then this autopsy report, Mr. Registrar, would receive what number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the autopsy report shall be given exhibit number P1253. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections against admission of this autopsy report?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. P1253 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The next document is 65 ter 6190, if we could have an exhibit number for this please, and if it could be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm always confused if we're talking about numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: This is the evidence sheet, Mr. President. That accompanied the autopsy report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- would receive number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document shall be given exhibit number P1254. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Then P1254 is admitted into evidence. The photograph, which will be marked for identification for the time being.

utterances.text: And that, Mr. Registrar, would receive?

utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given exhibit number P1255.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1255 is marked for identification in order to give an opportunity to the Defence to further verify. Could I just ask one question about the photograph just shown which is still on our screen. Do we see the four -- are these three or four vertebrae on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there are four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The two are the two on top. That's -- it looks like one, but these are two actually.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The top two are sitting on top of each other. And then C-1, C-2, and then C-3, C-4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. I just have one final section to deal with Dr. Clark which is the presentation of some photographs which are illustrative of the various findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would that need?

utterances.text: Then I suggest that we first have the break. If it would have been a couple of minutes, I would suggest that we continue our first session. We will have a break, and we will resume at ten minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, please proceed.

utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I'd now like to present to the witness a series of photographs. It's presented as a package, and my intent is to get -- to ask for one exhibit number for the package of 27 photographs, and effectively that will deal with 14 of the photographs that are the subject of the 25 November 2008 order, and we'll deal with the rest of the documents once they're all uploaded to e-court. This is a submission which is intended to be illustrative of various materials that were available to Dr. Clark and various different observations that he made of the remains. So, Mr. President, if I could please have 65 ter 6778 brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, these are the photographs that I received last night that they were going to be used with -- endeavored to try to find if they had been, in fact, been disclosed. I would like some guidance from him because it wasn't forthcoming in what had been produced to us, what had been admitted, and what had not pursuant to the submission to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The reason that this package is put together and provided last night is obviously that we met with Dr. Clark yesterday and we determined what would be a helpful set of illustrative photographs to explain -- just to provide exemplars of what is referred to the various autopsy reports and referred to in the expert report. I can go through each of the photographs in turn and indicate to my learned friend which ones have already been admitted, if -- if he would like me to do that now, or alternatively we can alternatively do that at the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm guided by what the Chamber would like me to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would think that for the sake of identifying these photographs other than from a KN number in this package, that might be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, we sent two documents over to the Defence last night. One of them was the set of photographs with the KN documents, and the second document was exactly the same document where the ERN numbers referenced so that we would not have this difficulty in course and that the Defence can do that reconciliation. I can give them the same document again. I can send that e-mail again, if that would help them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And pursuant to that exercise with the ERN numbers, I was unable to find that some of these had been disclosed that. That was my problem. I'm not trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I just wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the situation is Mr. Margetts says they were disclosed and just send a list and from two different angles in order to give you an opportunity to verify. You said, I was not able to verify. Of course, I have got no idea whether it is because they were not disclosed, whether you couldn't find it. I suggest that we proceed on the same basis as with the two photographs which certainly were not brought to your attention, although I think we saw only one of them, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. You did see only one of them. There was a second one I decided not to call.
