utterances.text: You decided -- but I suggest that we proceed on the same basis, and if there's any problem as far as lack of disclosure is concerned, if there's any other problem in relation to that, we'll resolve that, and they will be marked for identification for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further submissions by the Defence teams. If not, then, Mr. Margetts, please proceed on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you would allow me a just one moment of explanation. Obviously when we're talking about Prosecution files or we're talking about reporting records or we're talking about exhumation reports and other documentation relative to -- to killings and deaths, we're talking about hundreds if not thousands of documents. And it's been a feature of this case that we have cooperated well with the Defence in terms of assisting each other, in handling these materials, and I actually am not of the view that that my learned friend's comments today have accurately reflected a lot of the correspondence that's gone between the Prosecution and Defence on this matter. A lot of the correspondence has been the Defence indicating they had materials and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't notice anything of an unfriendly nature at this moment, so I take it that the good spirit will continue also on from this 12th of January. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, if we could please have 65 ter 6778 presented to -- on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, you'll see before you two photographs, and that is on page marked X023-0559. And under the heading pre-burial. Could you indicate to the Court -- firstly, could you look at the top photograph, and could you indicate to the Court whether that photograph was available to you at the time that you were preparing your reports.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Can I -- firstly, an apology that the problems with the photographs may be partly mine, in that normally I would have inserted photographs into the autopsy report -- the pathologist report, but the time scale was such that I could not do that, and these were also impossible because of the size to e-mail earlier so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Clark, there is no reason to make apologies in this respect, so the Chamber does understand and does appreciate that would you have liked to make our life even more comfortable, but don't start apologising, there's no need for that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, available to me in compiling my report, final report, were two types of photographs. One was a set of photographs which had been made available to us at the time of the autopsies. We weren't entirely sure where they came from. And I said in my report that they were interesting and informative, but I based very little on them. The second set of photographs are, of course, the autopsy photographs that we took in the mortuary which I can very much verify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, if I can just stop you there. If we refer to page 3 of your report and to the comments that you make. Actually, referring to page 2, and it's the top of page 2. You say that there were photographs that were taken in the past showing bodies prior to burial, some lying in the open and others laid out in the already excavated grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Registrar, if you could just pan out, please, on the photographs that are displayed on this pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: These exemplars of a photograph of somebody lying in the open and a body in an already excavated grave.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please move on to the second page, that's the last four digits 0560.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Dr. Clark, if you can just briefly identify the top two photographs and what they indicate.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. These are photographs from, the autopsy photographs, from the person in the lower photograph. And so they are -- I mean, I can explain the injuries if you want, but they are just to show the linkage between the two. We have pre-burial photographs, and we have autopsy photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Dr. Clark, if could you just explain what you derived from studying this skull.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Very briefly, top left photograph there is an arrow just to the left of the midline of the centre of the photograph. Just below that, there's a semi-circle going into a larger defect, that's a gunshot entrance hole, so that's into the back of the head. The next photograph on top right is looking at the front of the skull, the front of the face, and you will see that the entire face is missing, and this is the exit of this shot. So it's a shot just to the back of the head, just to the left of the midline coming out and blowing out of the face.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark. If we could now move on to the next page which is the last four digits 0561. And Dr. Clark, if you could deal first with the picture on the left, then move to the picture on the right at the top, and then the picture at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: These relate to a paragraph in the pathologist report. Effectively the top -- top of page 5 in which I discuss the difficulty in the interpretation of injuries and how we decide whether a particular body damage is a gunshot injury or could be something else, and there are various levels of certainty. The photograph on the top left I thinks is an absolute classic gunshot entrance hole in the top of the skull and fractures reading at about -- round about. There is no doubt at all what has caused that. Slightly less certain, photograph on the top right, this the top of your shin bone, the tibia, and it has been put together because it was in fragments, being glued together. And you can see just below the arrow a dark defect which is probably again the entrance hole but a little bit less well defined than the one in the skull. And finally the photograph on the bottom, this is of somebody's femur, thigh bone, here there is no -- we didn't find a nice -- a classic round hole in the bone. But what it does show is the typical fragmentation pattern of a bone when hit by a bullet of high velocity. There is one at the top end which is the left end there. You can see damage there, but even more visually found is at the lower end of the femur to the right of the photograph where the bone is shattered. And these, to us, were the evidence we were looking for to show these were gunshot injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could move on to the next page, 0562.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And again, Dr. Clark, if you could deal with the top photograph and then the bottom photograph.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I have referred to injuries typical of high-velocity weapons which is more correctly called high energy transfer weapons, but high velocity is easier. This is a sort of typical pattern. Legs of a man who had been shot at least 14 times. And in the legs there are at least five, probably five separate gunshot injuries. And the bottom picture shows some of the -- well, shows the bullets or fragments of bullets which were recovered from his body, and these are typical of 6.60 millimetre diameter typical of high-velocity ammunition, so these two cases are linked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, are you able to say what type of weapon would have fired this high-velocity ammunition?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, we were informed the likely weapon was an AK-47 assault rifle. The bullet size certainly would fit with that, and we have no reason to doubt that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could move on to the next page marked 0563.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And again, Dr. Clark, if you could deal with the top photograph first.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: This is just to emphasis the huge destructive nature of high-velocity ammunition when it hits the body, particularly when it hits bone and particularly when it hits the skull. These two photographs are the same person. The upper photograph shows obviously the mortuary photograph, and you're looking at the right side of the skull which, even though it has been glued together, shows a huge defect towards the front which is the right side. That is the exit gunshot injury. If you look in the pre-burial photograph, and I have inserted a black arrow, down bottom left. You can you see that, to me, is brain tissue which is coming out of the side of the skull. Obviously a very damaged skull and corresponds with the upper photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark. If we could move on to the next page which is marked 05643. And if you could take these photos in the order that you think is most sensible and just indicate, if you could, the location on the page of the photograph that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Very briefly, these are just other examples of the type of damage that we found in the bones which led to us believe that gunshot injuries were the cause of death in that particular person. The top photo, top left is of the lower jaw, and the middle photograph on the left is the same person. That's the right collar-bone, and this was probably one shot going through the jaw, through the jaw on the left-hand side an ending up in the chest through the collar-bone. The bottom left corner photograph shows somebody's left arm and shows a shot is he shoulder which the right end and a shot at the elbow which is about the middle. Top right photograph is a shoulder-blade scapula most of which is missing, the lower half. Again, typical gunshot injury. And finally bottom right is the left femur. There's a right intact femur for comparison to the thigh bone. And the left femur shows obvious gunshot injury at the lower end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could move on to the next page which is 0565. And again, Dr. Clark, if you could indicate the position of the photos on this page as you're discussing them.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: One of the other things that we tried to determine in addition to establishing that these were gunshot injuries was to see if we could tell the direction of fire whether front of body, or from the back, or whatever. And the way that this can be done, in some bones at least, is to look at the detail of the damage to the bone. When a bone -- a bullet hits bone, the first edge that it hits just leaves a sort of circle or semi-circle. But on the inside of that bone, the other surface, you get a bevelling effect like a crater going away from it, and that is easiest to see on skulls, but this is a particularly good examples on the ribs. The top pictures shows two ribs which were -- obviously a bullet has gone between the ribs and has caused a semi-circle hole, the bottom of the upper one and the upper part of the low one with some fracturing that -- if you imagine the bullet going into the screen, into the page. Down below there are two pictures of the same case. It's a bit dark, but the one on the left is the bullet going in the same direction. In other words, into the screen, but on the other surface of that bone, I think can you see the sort of cratering, bevelling effect which indicates that the bullet is coming out towards me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And that is the inner surface photo on the right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You're making those final comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If we could now move, Mr. Registrar, please, to the next page which is 0566. And again, Dr. Clark, if you could discuss these two photos.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Again, this is it just an example of trying to determine direction. The upper photograph is somebody's lower jaw, mandible, taken from behind which is a view few people can envisage. And this is a bullet which has gone through the back of the neck and come out through the lower jaw. And the arrow in the upper photograph is showing the bullet exiting, going into the screen. The lower photograph is just another example to show the track of that bullet. It's the same case. The bone stacked on the right-hand side of the spine, the neck bones. And we're able to tell that this is a single shot to the back of the neck coming out through the mouth, the lower jaw in the midline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark. And, Mr. Registrar, if we could please move tonight next page, which is it 0567.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Another one just showing tracks of bullets. It's also emphasises the care that was taken with these reconstruction of the skills and the expertise of the anthropologists in doing this. Because initially these skulls are in fragments, but they have been glued together such that we can identify tracks. There is one tack going through the top of the head, that's the purple rod, and coming out the right side of the face. And the second shot, the red rod, is going through the left side of the jaw, that's the person's left, and coming out destroying the right side. So just an example of determining directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark. If we could move to the next page which is 0568.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: The -- by far the greatest number of gunshot injuries that we saw were what I call high-velocity gunshot injuries. And I've shown you typical examples of that. Every so often we found bullet-holes in the bone which did not have this fragmentation pattern and suggested to us either the use of a handgun which is much lower velocity, or the other possibility would be that this is a high-velocity bullet which had passed through someone else or something else first and lost a lot of energy before it goes in. I suspect the former is more likely. The upper photograph, the white arrow, just follow it. You see a semi-circle in the eye socket. The lower photograph is the back of the head. This is the exit from the back of the head showing a very clean circular hole with minimal disruption and compare that with the damage I've shown you to the other bones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If we could now move on to 0569, which is the next page.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: In addition to the high-velocity weapons, occasionally we found injuries to the bones which were typical of shrapnel. Of the Annex A cases, it has to be said that there was only one which showed convincing blast or shrapnel damage. There were other cases in other bodies, but this is the only one. And it is just -- it's difficult to describe, but there's an irregular area in the hip bone and a piece of shrapnel metal which is lying to the left of it was found with the body. I don't know whether that occurred before or after death, and the cause of death in this lady was given as unascertained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark. And now, Mr. Registrar, if we could please refer to the last page of this presentation, and that is page 0570. And, Dr. Clark, if you could explain these two photographs.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Occasionally we saw other types of injuries other than gunshot injuries. And two types: One is what we call blunt-force which is when the body is either hit by something solid or the person themselves hits something solid like a fall. In this case, 283, the upper photograph, you can see an area fracturing just above the outer part of the right eye socket, the orbit. It's got an arrow to it. And that was indicative to us of blunt force. It looked to -- this is a typical pattern that we see as general pathologists in our day-to-day work, and I think is very likely a blunt-force injury applied in life. The second photograph is unusual, and it's the only one of its kind. This is on the left side of the head, and there was a slicing through the bone which you can see with the arrow, and that's obviously been caused by some sort of sharp instrument. Now it takes something heavy and sharp to cut into the skull. I have suggested something like a machete or a similar heavy weapon. So these photographs are just to show, to illustrate the general findings in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Dr. Clark, can you confirm for the Court that you put this presentation together yesterday during the course of your meeting with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: The basis was already done, and we finished it yesterday, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark. That concludes my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if I could please have an exhibit number for this presentation marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Series of photographs, Mr. Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given exhibit number P1256. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Looking at the Defence, we should keep status of marked for identification. Then P1256 is marked for identification, and the Chamber would like to hear from the Defence as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Margetts. Mr. Clark, I developed a custom that I address everyone Mr., Mrs., whether you professor, general, or a monsignor. Just for you to explain, it's not any expression of not acknowledging your academic qualifications.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe is Defence counsel for Mr. Gotovina and will now cross-examine you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think we had the pleasure to meet up in the cafeteria some months back.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: We did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But it was quite brief. Doctor, I'm just going to go through a few things in your report and highlight a few others maybe to illuminate your report, so just say anytime we are not understanding each other or you don't understand me, please stop me, and I will attempt to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, you mentioned in your report the difficulties in making forensic analyses under the conditions such as you confronted in Knin because obviously these bodies had been in the ground for some time, and there was a significant amount of decomposition. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I think you also --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will go through this quickly. It's on page 3 of the witness's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you also mentioned that normally in the day-to-day affairs of a forensic pathologist, you have some degree of organ structure on a body which allows you to better ascertain angle of fire, possibly the level of damage that was in just the torso area and not the bone. Any number of pieces of information that you are unable to assess when just dealing with skeletal remains?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now in addition to that, I think you mentioned this morning, and that would be at -- excuse me. This afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: This afternoon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm getting my time a little off here. And I do believe I wrote this down in response to a question by Judge Orie --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: The dental.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It was on page 25 of the transcript, line 11 and 12. You were discussing post-mortem and pre-mortem injuries, antemortem and post-mortem injures, and you noted that often times it is almost impossible, and again this is on page 4 of your report, to make an assessment whether an injury was post- or pre-mortem item. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Because, I mean, I think again in your report -- and we're not going to repeat this. On page 4 you go through any number of injuries that happen to a body during the post-mortem simply by handling or by burying or by transporting, et cetera, right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I'm interested, though, in your comment on page 4 of your -- page 4, subparagraph 2 of your report. And this is last sentence, and you're talking about in the section deciding whether injuries found had occurred before or after death, and you discussed the difficulty in it. You note that in the end when -- this is the last sentence. Are you with me, Doctor? In the end, where there was doubt, the benefit of such doubt was given to the injury being post-mortem in nature."

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you were trying to that to be careful, is that right, sir, or --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. My question is with regard to the actual bodies themselves -- and let's go back to the next two paragraphs down beginning "strictly speaking." It says: "Strictly speaking, therefore, in these decomposed and often incomplete bodies with no soft tissues in which to see bruising and no body cavity in which to find internal bleeding or disrupted organs, it was virtually impossible to be certain that any injury found necessarily occurred in life. And theoretically, all of them could have occurred after death even the very often gunshot injuries."

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Well, conscious of this theoretical difficulty, the report is nevertheless compiled on the assumption that the vast majority if not all of the gunshot and other specified injures found in these bodies occurred in life, and that they were or contributed to the cause of death. To assume otherwise would make any future analyses of the findings meaningless." So just to clarify, Doctor, you made a decision that when you saw post injuries that if you couldn't determine if they were antemortem or post-mortem, you said that they were post-mortem. Yet when you saw these gunshot wounds, you assumed for the sake of your report that all of these gunshot wounds were antemortem. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. The ones that we raised out in -- we took the view that all gunshot wounds were antemortem. If you don't assume that, you have to assume that these are people who have died in some other way of which there is no evidence whatsoever on the bodies. And that not only that, but that the bodies were then shot after death. That is the alternative notion. Which is maybe possible, and that is for others to determine. If I can clarify the -- if the damage to the bones was typical of gunshot injury, and I have shown you plenty examples of that, then it's fairly straightforward. It is the -- when the damage is less convincing of gunshot and could be pressure effect on a bone, a broken rib which is far less typical of a gunshot injury, and we could -- was much more difficult to distinguish that from a post-mortem injury than from say from a blunt-force trauma. And we -- these are the sort of situations we erred on the post-mortem side. It is not so much the gunshot injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me go back to a scenario. And I'm not saying -- just when we look at this hypothetical that all of these situations fall into this category, but you can't, for instance, dispense with the possibility that somebody died in a hand-to-hand combat situation and that after the body was there, some person - and I'm not justifying the conduct - some person shot into that body after it was dead. And you can't discount that possibility because of the evidence that you were dealing with?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That's right. I can't discount that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I mean, does that account for your comment in the actual next comment when you were trying to determine the cause of a particular injury in discussing the difficulties: "The vast majority of the injuries found in these bodies were gunshot injuries or at least what were interpreted as such." Now, was that a -- a -- again, an assumption by you when you were looking at these injuries, and for lack of some other way to go, you just assumed that they were gunshot injuries?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, we -- I mean, gunshots do have a fairly typical pattern, and if it did have anything of the three that I have listed, then we attributed them to gunshot injuries. It was the ones in which there really was not very much just a broken bone, no bullet fragments, then we doubted whether that was genuine gunshot or not. And these are the ones that we erred on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just bear with me for one second, Doctor, but it appears from this sentence that you are possibly erring in the other direction where you say: "The vast majority of the injuries in these bodies were gunshots injuries or at least what were interrupted as such."

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, first of all, that has been asked an answered; and, second of all, it would be helpful if the clarifying sentences were read with that sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let me just ... just something was put to the witness in the last question and no question followed yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and I'd say that that has already been put to him at page 48, lines 18 to 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe can put whatever question in relation to what he again put to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, on that particular issue - and I'm just trying to get from assistance from you on this - it would appear that when you saw an injury that could have been or could have not been a gunshot injury, you interpreted as a gunshot injury?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. The ideal situation is clearly there is skin and soft tissue and the whole body, and if we saw that plus the damage to the bone, then that is a gunshot injury. All we have here is bones, largely, so we are already missing 50 per cent of the evidence. So on the basis of the damage to the bone, I'm interpreting that as a gunshot injury. That's where the level of doubt is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But there is that level of doubt in your mind based on the evidence that you were presented with?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In fact, Doctor, in your report on page -- and now if we move to the cause of death in your report at page 5, you note under the circumstances where there is no surrounding tissue and internal organs: "It was therefore seldom possible to strictly prove a precise cause of death, only to imply it."

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, in fact, Doctor, in coming up with this precise cause of death, you, in fact, disagree -- and I'm -- take this from your supplemental information sheet. You disagree or qualify the conclusions made by your fellow pathologists who were examining some of these bodies at the mortuary -- at the mortuary in Zagreb, did you not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: We seldom disagreed. I think I know what you're meaning, but that it is just a few, and that has been done on reviewing of the cases later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm just taking this from your supplemental information sheet, and if we can just take a look at -- on two, if we can bring up 65 ter 6184, I'm not certain that that's been received in evidence, but I will just deal with the 65 ter number at this junction. But it has to do with KN01/204.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could bring that up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for the witness's information, the reference to the supplemental information sheet I think I indicated to Dr. Clark during the course of proofing that additional information here provided to the Office of the Prosecutor would be put in a written form and provided to the Defence, and I just him to be clear that that's what Mr. Kehoe is referring to when referring to the supplemental information sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We have an autopsy -- we can just deal with the primary sheet. This is by Doctor --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Maria de Mendonca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm not going to attempt to pronounce that. However, it denotes where in the second paragraph on this individual there were multiple comminuted fractures to the left rib, 6; right rib, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10. These findings are neither consistent with nor indicative of being caused by ballistic influence. And ballistic influence of bullets, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But by blunt trauma of the chest, and the cause of death is blunt trauma to the chest. And I note that in your information that you gave to Office of the Prosecutor during your proofing back in December, you told the Prosecutor that the person may have died of either blunt trauma to the chest or possibly by gunshot to the chest area. Now, my question to you, Doctor, is not to determine who is right and who is wrong, but there is a high degree of subjectivity in this. And the reality is on this particular autopsy, you had some disagreement or doubt with the pathologist who actually examined this body, did you not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: The disagreement, if you like, or questioning I think is a better word, only came when I was reviewing all the cases. It was not in the mortuary at the time because I cannot remember that. But well, I had the benefit of going through huge numbers of autopsies. I had the benefit of having had two years previously -- for the past previous two years working this sort of material, and I am -- I just felt that the injuries here were not dissimilar to injuries seen in gunshot -- other gunshot cases. And I just question it. You will also note that I have not changed the cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You didn't examine this body?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I didn't examine it, nor I don't think there were there any photographs taken of it, so it was difficult to review.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's take a look at another one which is 65 ter 6248. I do believe that is admitted already. I'm not certain given the listing of things if these items have been admitted or not. I mean I don't want to certainly do -- multiply these documents, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The problem apparently is that in the 25th of November decision, the OTP is invited to put all those documents that were not yet admitted on a list so that numbers could be assigned to it. Now, Mr. Margetts, did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that hasn't happened as yet, and so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that causes the problem now that we are assigning numbers not knowing whether they are admitted or not because that is what the last part of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can inform the Court and the parties that all of the autopsy reports referred to the annexes to Dr. Clark's export report have been admitted but haven't been assigned numbers. So I think that -- it would be our recommendation that the most convenient way to proceed would be for numbers to be assigned as and when they are presented, and obviously that that will alleviate the need to assign numbers to those autopsy reports at a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it could have been done already since the 25th of November, that's six weeks ago. And you say now we take out the ones we're using at this moment. We assign numbers to them and whatever remains then will be on your list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we did commence work on this breaking each of -- we had large 65 ter numbers consisting of thousands of pages, and we have been breaking those down into smaller 65 ter numbers and uploading them, not only autopsy reports but identification against Croatian reports and other materials as well so yes, it would been a better situation if we had been able to provide those table in accordance with the order, but I can assure, Mr. President, that we have been working on it, and we're very close to finishing that process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean by this week, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I mean by this week, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Margetts, then we expect the list, and then of course as was said in the 25th November decision only documents that were not yet admitted so you keep a good record of what is admitted now so that these documents do not again appear then on your list which we expect by this Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I do believe that I said -- I believe I'm not sure. I think it is part of that list, but if I can just operate with the 65 ter numbers until we get to some clarity on whether or not they are in or not. Or I could just put it in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't understand we're talking about. The autopsy report in relation to KNO0, 204 B which bears the police ID number 504 when I'm well-informed, which actually speaks of a blunt trauma chest. And, Mr. Margetts, you assure us that all these autopsy reports appear in the A to D annexes underlying the 25th of November decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, all of the autopsies reports referred to in annexes to Mr. Clark's expert report have been admitted into evidence. Secondly, we provided the Defence with a listing and a referencing to the appendices that are referenced in the 25 November order, so if my learned friend refers to the exhibit list, he will be able to see the listing on the left-hand side. And then whether or not they're admitted appears in the far corner of the list we've provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... just for sake of clarity and for the transcript as to keeping track of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Questions were put to the witness in relation to this autopsy report. I take it that you wanted it to be a D number assigned to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, this report which is numbered case number KN01 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 6184.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now -- yes, as a matter of fact -- yeah. I was dealing with the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 6184 is KN204 [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 204 B. Yes. Okay. That was the previous one which we saw on the screen. Mr. Registrar, the autopsy report KN01/204 B which has been shown to the witness previously will have number, Defence number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document shall be given exhibit number D1221. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1221 was already admitted into evidence but now continues its evidentiary life as D1221. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm going to turn to yet another autopsy report for KN01/281, which is 65 ter 6248. Again, it's on the screen. And again if we go to the last -- or actually first -- fourth paragraph we have a findings that are neither consistent nor indicative of being caused by ballistic influence and by -- but by blunt trauma to the chest and pelvis. There were no other kind of trauma to the bones and the cause of death is blunt trauma to the chest and pelvis. And again in your supplemental information sheet you took issue with this and noted that the damage to the spinal column and vertebrae suggest that this death was caused by gunshot injury. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I knew these cases would cause problems, but they have to be taken in the context of all of other cases. I looked at this report and felt that describing comminuted fractures. Now comminuted means a bone which is broken into several bits in the spine, is a very uncommon injury in -- with blunt force trauma as we see it, either somebody being hit by something or even somebody falling, or even a road accident. It is it a very uncommon injury, and I felt in the context of all the other cases that an injury like that, breaking up a bone is probably more likely gunshot damage. However, you will note that I did not change -- well, I changed the cause of death but put it unascertained because I felt that we could not decide particularly easily. So the cause of death is -- I think now should probably be unascertained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, in fact, you did change Dr. Mendonca's conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I have not changed the post-mortem report, the autopsy report, and that stands. And that she can be questioned on it if need be, but doing my summary report, that I just taking everything into consideration I felt that that was probably more likely to be gunshot damage. I'm sure if we had discussed it at the time in the mortuary, we may have come to -- I don't know what decision we would have come to, but we could have discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'd like to offer 65 ter 6248 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is the supplemental information sheet?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that is the next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... the next autopsy report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Which is already admitted into evidence. It just needs a number assigned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would be a D number, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be D number 1222. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1222, the Chamber establishes that it is it already admitted, and that it will further carry this number. Now let me just check ... yes, that supplemental information sheet, is that available to this Chamber because you're referring to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It hasn't been, Judge, but we have no objection with it being made available to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I am a bit confused. In the supplemental information sheet we're supposed to find -- we do not know exactly the reasons that it was rather a gunshot injury than -- than blunt trauma, and on the list attached to the report, we find unascertained cause the death which are -- we have now three options.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have uploaded the supplemental information sheet. We can bring it up and then just move it into evidence so Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because otherwise we are missing a portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, is there any problem in uploading that, since it now gives a bit more. It gives a third option for the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It has been uploaded, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Supplemental information to be tendered by you, Mr. Margetts?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, possibly it would be worthwhile having the witness review that supplemental information sheet given --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it will be marked for identification for the time being and then we might ask you to do some homework, Mr. Clark. If a hard copy would be available, and if -- do we have for the supplemental information sheet, do we have a 65 ter number? Has it been uploaded already?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have uploaded it. 1D64-0011.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1D64-0011. Perhaps if it has been uploaded by the Defence let's give it -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document shall be given exhibit number D1223. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if that could be marked for identification pending the witness's review of that sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, D1223 is marked for identification, a hard copy should be given to Mr. Clark. And Mr. Clark, you're invited to review that supplemental information sheet in which the last minute information is usually reflected to see whether there are any matters which you find not correct. If you could do that over night, so that we could hear from you tomorrow. And which party is going to provide Mr. Clark with the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: We will do that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you provide it to the registry, then it will be given to Mr. Clark. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, I raise these issues not to question the good faith of everybody involved, but simply, this highlights what you were saying in your report on page 5. It says: "Seldom possible to strictly prove the precise cause of death." And people can look at this in different ways. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, I noted during the course of your direct examination -- and bear with me if I don't have the exact numbers. I noted that you had, for instance, been in Srebrenica. And I think you noted there were six different locations that you examined and --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: At least six yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I think you didn't mention this, but I do believe I think I read in some of your correspondence that you, in fact, were looking at graves that had been disturbed and changed and bodies hidden, et cetera. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, a few were like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in this discussion you were examining bodies that were in a cemetery in Knin.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: A much different situation, for instance, than what you were presented with in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: In some of the cases. Some of the sites in Srebrenica were primary graves and not dissimilar to this one, other than -- here I gather that the bodies were laid out, where in Srebrenica, they were jumbled on top of each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The bodies in this situation were laid out?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now we have heard much talk. And by witnesses not much talk. There has been talk by witnesses of this cemetery being a mass grave, and for the sake of the Chambers reference, that would be pages 10661, line 7 through 10666, line 25, the testimony of Mr. William Hayden. Now these bodies that were laid out in an orderly fashion were not -- well, let's just talk about it. These bodies that were laid out often times were in coffins, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Some of them were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Some were in plastic bags, right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Some of them had identification numbers on them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: The majority in KN01 had identification labels.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Some of them even had viles of blood around their neck?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Blood bottles. No blood in them. Blood bottles with a name in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With the name of the person?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So this particular cemetery was a cemetery that, you concluded, was set out not to hide these bodies from the international community such as you might have found in Srebrenica, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I don't think that is a question for me to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the basis is for asserting to Dr. Clark that's what he concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness answered the question by saying that he doesn't think it is a question for him to answer. Apparently he considers it to be beyond his expertise. But of course you can ask questions of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I would refer to your report that -- and you say in page 11 of your report that it has to be remembered also that these were all bodies from a normal cemetery and so may have been there before the incident being investigated.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So first and foremost, this was not a cemetery that you concluded as a forensic pathologist would contain bodies that were being hidden. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I follow that. I mean, I barely saw the cemetery. I wasn't involved in the exhumation. I don't know what -- how you could interpret degree of hiding or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I'm not sure there is much more I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me take it one step further. It certainly wasn't a cemetery such as you found -- possibly found in Srebrenica or may have heard about in Iraq where people were executed in the grave in a seriatim fashion or pushed into the ground and then dirt pulled over them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yeah. It's my understanding and based -- to some extent on the photographs, the pre-burial photographs, that these were bodies placed deliberately into a grave, killed elsewhere, and placed into a grave in a relatively neat order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you concluded it was in a relatively neat order, you took into consideration that these bodies were numbered and laid out in an orderly fashion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. You can see that in the photographs there. The ones in the grave any way are lined up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me talk with you a little bit about some of the circumstances and the injuries that we have. Now you note on page 24 of your report that of the assumed 245 genuine cases, 202 had died of gunshot wounds; 6, 2.5 per cent, from blast injuries; one from blunt force trauma and a knife to the head, and the remaining 35 were those dying from causes unknown. Now, let's deal with the gunshot injuries. The gunshot injuries that you saw -- in many cases were from high-velocity rounds?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And high-velocity rounds I think you told us were a 7.26 round coming out of a AK-47?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: These are the type of injuries that you expect to see in war, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. Well, partly. More often in war you will find many more explosive injuries than bullet injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But dealing with the gunshot injuries because we'll get to the blast injuries as well.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: In terms of gunshot injuries, yes, that is the sort of injury you would expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just going a little further in your report. Again I'm staying on page 24 for a bit, where you talk about the use of high-velocity rounds. You note that there was no particular pattern to the shots then the majority being to the trunk, the largest surface area of the body, and striking the body from a variety of different directions. Now, that assessment, Doctor, is consistent with an assaulting army shooting at the enemy with an attempt to putting that enemy on the ground. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: It could be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, that is it normally what the use of an AK-47 is, isn't it, to spit out a significant amount of high-velocity rounds to put the enemy on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, of course, yes. I thought you were implying about direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand that the direction of fire becomes a difficult assessment?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But all I'm getting at here, is you have of your 245 genuine cases, and 202 dying of gunshot rounds --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- most of those people died of high-velocity -- of high-velocity rounds. Most of them took shots to the trunk area, and that type of shooting is consistent with an armed combat of people moving or shooting in a direction against the enemy.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That pattern is. There was also a pattern of a certain number of cases in which single gunshot injury to the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We'll get to that in a second because we have some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, may I ask you to make the usual pauses between -- because the transcriber has some difficulties in following your relatively high speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Apologies, apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wouldn't say high energy, but high velocity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, you speak with a Scottish accent and I speak Brooklynese. And there is some difficulty going back and forth, so I will take a pause between a question and answer. I'm sorry, did you finish your last answer?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you also note that - again this is it on page 24 - 28 per cent of the people appear to be killed by a single shot. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you say a single shot, and this includes shots to the cranium or wherever, the difficulty you have with that is that if there is an shot to the cranium, which, based on your analysis, may be the death shot.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It can take into account possibly multiple other shots to the torso which you may not find because all you're dealing with is skeletal remains?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That may account for a small number, but really a shot to the torso unless it's in a very small area in the abdomen on either side is going to leave damage on the bone. You have a very short space between your ribs and your hip bone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I mean -- let me -- let me qualify that as the torso. Let me say the trunk. If we have a shot to the head and spraying AK-47 rounds to the head and some the trunk and people are taking -- a soldier is taking several rounds to the trunk, in a very short order, that person will bleed out. And when you look at the body, you may only see the shots to the head and may not see what could be the fatal injury which is a shot to the actual trunk.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, remember your spine goes down the back of your trunk all the way. As I say there is a very signal area on either sides of the abdomen on which there is no soft tissue from front to back, and, yes, I have admitted that, but we could be missing a few shots, but I would doubt very much if it was a huge number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. And I understand that, but that is also a factor in this equation which makes the actual cause of death very uncertain?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I think maybe you should get away from cause of death because the important thing is the number of injuries or the fact that they have been shot. The cause of death to some extent is subsidiary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go -- I apologise. Then I will take your lead and just say, that it calls into question the number of shots that an individual body took on when that person was shot.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, we are -- trying to estimate as well -- as best we could the minimum of shots to each person, and on the one hand, we've got to balance missing a shot through a soft tissue like the abdomen or the thigh, but, at the same time, what we interpreted as one shot damaging maybe two parts of the body could easily be one. So I think there is a balance on either side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, Doctor, I understand the difficulties with being -- doing this examination so far done the line. But it does become difficult to make the assessment as to the number of shots even if someone only has one shot to the cranium.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. Which is why I put minimum number. That's the ones that I can -- I'm fairly happy about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The next issue I just want to talk briefly about and to clarify this, and that goes to actually when this -- these -- these killings, deaths, if you will, transpired because there are some people that died of natural causes, of course, some people that died of gunshot wounds.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: With respect we don't know that people died of natural causes. I can only speculate at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We'll get to that. We have a few of those. We'll get to that. Now, you note -- at page 1 of your report that the mortuary team had fairly limited information -- page 1, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "The mortuary team had fairly limited information about the cases but were aware that they were said to have included alleged victims of Operation Storm, the military offensive reported to have been carried out against the Serb population in the Krajina region of Croatia from August to November 1995." Now, Doctor, were you made aware that there was combat between the Serb forces and the Croatian forces, the HV, throughout the winter of 1994 and throughout 1995 through various operations up until approximately July the 28th of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: We weren't specifically made aware. I'm aware that that -- since that that is a possibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And did you inquire as to where the Serb soldiers who were killed in that operation were buried?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No. I mean you could take the argument that the less information that we are given as -- in the mortuary, the better because we can be more independent. I mean some people will take that view, and I think -- if we were given a great deal of specific information that may well could prejudice us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It could help as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: It could help.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: But that perhaps could come at a later date in reviewing the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's take that. It could come at a later date, and you are looking at these bodies. There was no way for you to determine, was there, which Serbs -- which individuals in that grave had been killed in combat prior to the 4th and the 5th of August. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: None at all, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And let's take the outside of Operation Storm and say it went from the 4th to the 8th of August, given at the outside a date. There was no way for you to make a determination when you did the exhumation and your forensic work which bodies in that grave were buried in there or died after combat operations had ended in Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No. I have no detailed information of the grave site.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You couldn't tell the difference. Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, I -- I raise this point for this issue, and if I can turn your attention to your annex for KN01, and I present this at -- on page 13. And I address you to the KN01/307 B to 315. Do you see those, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One begins Dusan, Djukic. And then there are a whole bunch of Beric's. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: According to the evidence presented to this Court and the clarification schedule that was presented by the Office of the Prosecutor to the Chamber, these are events that took place in Varivode on the 28th of September of 1995. Now, were you informed that these deaths occurred approximately 28th of September 1995, well after the Operation Storm matters were over?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No. I mean, at the time of the autopsies, we had no identify about identification. Identification of the bodies only came later on. So we had no idea who was who. We could not identify a particular body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let me take it one step further and move ahead from after the actual time when you were doing the forensic analysis at the morgue in Zagreb until thereafter. When you were going through and presenting your reports or having discussions with the Office of the Prosecutor as late as yesterday, did you have discussions that deaths such as that had occurred well after?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we look just at these -- and there are others. We can go into them if you want to. But if you look just at these, in dealing with the Varivode situation, there are at least four of that list were single shots to the head.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you were -- and I'm talking about since the 2001 -- in trying to flesh out the work that you have done, did you ask the Prosecutor if the Republic of Croatia had done any investigation on this matter so that you could have the benefit of findings that they had made so you could maybe more accurately assess your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No. I don't think that's our role. I mean, certainly not the way that I'm used to practicing autopsy reports and giving evidence in the -- in the UK courts. It is our job to present the findings from the autopsy, and, if it is put to you certain scenarios, as you are doing at the moment, I'm happy to agree or disagree. But it is not my role to initiate investigations, unless it is something very peculiar and difficult to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And my statement to you, Doctor, is I'm not disagreeing with that. I'm just saying that type of situation where an investigation had in fact been conducted in some fashion by the Republic of Croatia prior to coming in here to testify today, none of that information had been presented to you for your review to see if, in some fashion, additional information could clarify or sharpen some of your conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe the Chamber wonders, you're putting a lot of information to the witness, for example, this one, whereas the Chamber does not understand the report to say anything about when exactly these people died, whether they died from gunshot injuries by -- during a combat operation, outside the context of a combat operation. We find nothing you put to the witness at this moment as part of the report. I think the report describes the findings and the difficulties in making any determination. And I take it if you could have made determinations on the basis of your expertise, which went beyond what we find here, that you would have indicated so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, if not, that you were not able to do -- to make such determinations, such as whether the context --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you are putting a lot of things to the -- Mr. Clark, yes, which seems not to be part of what he has presented here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We will go into yet further. I mean, if I can ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if it brings us somewhere --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It will bring us -- it will bring us, Judge, because we will -- if you bear with me, Judge, there are numerous items here that we will go into concerning what the Office of the Prosecutor has presented to the Chamber as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What the Chamber understands has been presented at this moment is the findings of Mr. Clark. That is, what he found on a skull, whether he found any clothing on the bodies, these kind of things, and not anything more. So therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There is a lot more, Judge. This is a lot more. I mean, that -- in presenting Dr. Clark with additional information as a forensic pathologist, that he should have been informed of. There is a lot more and a lot of these that -- as we go through them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, until now, we haven't -- just for argument's sake, if Mr. Clark would have known that there would have been an investigation about a Varivode event, either prior to or after, what -- in what way would that have changed any of his findings or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Very simply. In his report -- I'll answer that question. It would have given Dr. Clark a time range as to when events took place. Now, quite clearly, Varivode is well outside of Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But is there -- was Mr. Clark, was he focussing on timing of the cause of death? Is that part of what he presents to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is always a part of a forensic pathologist's determination. In this instance, it's a very difficult scenario to approach because of the time, because of the decomposition of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's ask Mr. Clark: Did you focus, in your expertise, on the time at which death occurred in these cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Clearly these people had not died in the previous few weeks, and they had been clearly dead for a considerable time. Whether that was three years, four years, five years, longer, I do not know, and I certainly could not at any stage tell that it was four years, seven months, or four years nine months. It has come over to me and to others in all our work in these mass graves how variable the preservation of bodies are. And you can see in this grave we have some bodies which are fully -- well, fully intact and other ones that are completely skeletonized, how we can tell time of death, well, I know we can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You can't.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No.
