utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, do we have any Latin interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's not Latin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is typed in is Latin, and what is pre-printed seems to be -- but we could ask -- it says uzroks mrti [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The Latin is different in the two. That's what I am getting at. If you see the Latin in 18 in the English, and you see the Latin of 89 in the B/C/S, the original, it is different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is what Mr. Clark drew our attention to, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think this is Latin. I think with respect, it's B/C/S. I recognise that vulnis capitarium [phoen] from my work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that seems to be the Latin part, the medical Latin part, and is there any problem with the translation of what we read in English to be the cause of death and then copy from the death certificate? Is there any problem with that, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There is no problem with the death certificate being a gunshot wound to the head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let me see that the translation of words in Latin in the original B/C/S is translated in a different Latin in the English version. That would be my provisional conclusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have thought somebody in the Court must be able to translate what that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that it is a mistake, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think it's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Suffice it to say, Doctor, this individual, this Radomir Bojanic, KN01/213 died of a gunshot wound -- you assume he died of a gunshot wound to the head?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, we will correct it, but we will offer into evidence 1D64-0042.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? Or same, you would like to look at it first? Then we will have it marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the -- these are documents that the witness has not seen, and the witness is not able to make any comments on other than to say that he hasn't seen them, and he is not being invited to make any comments on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We could -- it seems to me that until now we are always talking about people dying on or before the 4th of August. Is that the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That was one issue with them. This issue is quite different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This issue is quite different?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Quite different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then you were not informed about the content of this document at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at all, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No time whatsoever? So then it will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'd -- my submission would be that if we're going to proceed with presenting these documents in this way, and the witness isn't able to add anything to them, then it would be better if they were dealt with as a bar table submission. If alternatively there is a need to put them to the witness to see whether they corroborate or contradict the report, then I would invite my learned friend to do that, or I will alternatively --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is clear that until now that the main purpose of putting it to the witness is that the Defence apparently has in its possession this information which is from a -- apparently from a different source and which gives information that was unknown to the witness when he drafted his reports or at any later stage. Now, to the extent that on the earlier ones, we're talking about the 2nd of August, that would have been a matter which I take it just to establish that there are documents which put the date of death earlier than the 4th of August could have been, I take it, easily been established or agreed upon, as well as that this witness had -- has never received any information about this. I mean, do we have to go -- but you say this one is different, so I'm waiting and we'll look at what is different in this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Can we have these marked for identification, Your Honour, at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, The number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document shall be given exhibit number D1231, marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1231 keeps that status for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, we noted from the prior document, and I think that in the course of looking at 213 which is the autopsy report, you had this individual's clothing was camouflage. Can you concluded that this was a military person, did you not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you just by way of clarifying this, and if I can take -- show you D -- page from D930. And this is a book by an ARSK soldier Marko Vrcalj called: "The war for Serbian Krajina." And that's the front page, Doctor, and I know you haven't seen this before, but I want you to read one portion of, and I wanted to ask you some questions based on your autopsy and the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could go to page 9 in the English and page 8 in the B/C/S. I think it's on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First some clarification, Mr. Kehoe. You put it to the witness that you concluded that this was a military person, did you not, and in the report I read "possibly" which is not the same as the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Possibly a military person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Possibly a military person. Okay. Please proceed. Is that what your conclusion was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can I go to page 9 of the English and page 8 of the B/C/S, and I need to go to the top of the page. I think we have one further page on the English, please. It should be 10 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can just read. And this is a book by an ARSK General, Doctor, in Knin, that's writing about the events of the 4th. And I can reference it for you, but suffice it to say that when he says that afternoon in the first paragraph -- that is the 4th of August. "That afternoon, Colonel Bojanic from the RV PVO air force and anti-aircraft had committed suicide in his office because he couldn't stand all this." Now, I take it that that information was not given to you at any point prior to today that there was evidence that Colonel Bojanic committed suicide?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, and I understand you have to work with what you have, but with this information if we look back at D1230 which is your autopsy, this comment by Mr. Vrcalj is consistent with your assessment, that is, of someone, in this case, probably a right-handed person putting a pistol to his head and committing suicide, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I'm not sure if we can say it was a pistol, but it was quite extensive damage which would rather go against a pistol shot. More likely to be a rifle, I would have thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, if someone shot a .45 to the side of their head, it would have significant damage, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Not on the same scale I think as we found. I can't remember the details, but I'd have to look up the report again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you want to go back to look at the report. You can.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Which is D1230.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: If we can go on to the second page of that, please. And the third -- the third page and up a bit. That's fine. Well, that fracturing part suggests a high-velocity injury. Talk about large defect, radiating fractures, large exit defect, fragmentation to the upper part of the face, that very much suggested high velocity. That doesn't mean to say that he could not have used a rifle to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That doesn't mean say he couldn't use a .45 and cause that kind of damage, a .45-caliber weapon would cause extensive damage if one shot oneself in the side of the head.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: It would cause a hole going through, coming out the other side. I'm not sure it would cause the degree of fragmentation that we've seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you don't have any reason to believe that this conclusion, this statement, by Colonel Vrcalj is -- can be assistant with what you saw at the time, isn't it, that the guy committed suicide?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: It is consistent, it's not specifying which weapon was used, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, is this the type of information when you're making a conclusion that someone in this instance was beat up and then in all intents and purposes executed. Is this the type of information that you would want to factor into the equation before you came to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No. I mean I think the proper way of doing it is as we are doing. I have given my views in the report. You're now putting various scenarios to me which I am agreeing or disagreeing with. I'm quite happy to do that. But if I was to look at every individual case, where do I stop? How do I go about getting that information? That is not my task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: But I'm happy to agree with scenarios put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I guess just taking it one step further, I mean, you have been here several times, here in The Hague, and the Prosecution has never shown you this item on Colonel Bojanic, right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let us turn our attention to a -- by the way before we go to this -- let's go to this one first. And if we can bring up 65 ter 6325.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, what are we going to do with the part of the book, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, it's in evidence already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hope you do not mind that I do not have all the pages already in my mind which is and which is not admitted into evidence. Could you give me the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D930, and can we --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Page 9 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 9 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 10 in the English, 8 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, this is -- this is the autopsy report that we talked about just very briefly that you discussed in your report. It is a woman, and it notes that there was an apparent blindfold - it's in the second paragraph - made from a piece of blue cloth. There were also ropes around the body or at least partly around it, a double length of thick white cord around the chest and right upper arm and thicker piece of rope lying free under it at the back of the chest. Whether they represented true ligatures or bindings or were applied to the body after death to ease of movement is very difficult to say. Moving down, the only injuries present were what appeared to be post-mortem fractures of the face, larynx, and most of the ribs on the left side of the chest. There were no obvious bullet injuries or other antemortem trauma. The general lack of findings and despite the presence of the blindfold, it is not possible from this examination to say how the woman died. Now I take it -- this is, in fact, yours. And I will tell that you this was a body according to the Prosecutor that was retrieved on the 22nd of September, 1995. And if I direct your attention to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would like to offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, this has already been admitted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it now receives then a number. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document receives the number D1232. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1232, autopsy report relating to case number KN01/327 B was already admitted into evidence, and will bear that number. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can turn our attention to 65 ter 723. This is a two-page document concerning KN01/327. I'm sorry, I think I have the wrong number here, Judge. Okay. If we can just look at that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That document reflects that, on the 22nd of September, 1995, this document was retrieved from a well.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: The body was retrieved from a well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The body was retrieved from a well. Excuse me. The body was retrieved from a well. Had you seen this particular document when you were doing your examination, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No. I saw none of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'd like to offer into evidence 65 ter 723.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we will have to check whether or not that has already been admitted into evidence. I'm assured it hasn't been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... appears one of the documents that was not tendered by the Prosecution, or is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: It's already admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So it just needs a number. It was part of Appendix A to the Prosecution's motion, so it only needs a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given exhibit number 1233. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1233 was already admitted into evidence and is now identified under this number. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, when you were looking at this document, did you consider that this woman committed suicide?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's look at P320, which is a document that the Prosecution put into evidence concerning a Mrs. Stegnjaic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could go into private session on this. I note --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into -- we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Kehoe, for you, until the end of the first session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I hear from other Defence counsel. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will have no more than 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No more than 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, I just looked at some of this, and I think I will probably go into the second session. I apologise, but I think I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But from I understand, that there is no way that Mr. Clark could not be excused tomorrow. Then ... yes. I didn't see you, Mr. Mikulicic, when Mr. Kehoe was standing, so I apologise for addressing you as Mr. Kuzmanovic, who, apparently, is not present today. We will adjourn until tomorrow, Tuesday, the 13th of January, quarter past 2.00 in this same Courtroom I, but not until I have instructed you not to speak with anyone about the testimony, whether already given or still to be given tomorrow, Mr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
